query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase FCC high-/medium-entropy alloys whose stacking-fault energy (SFE) lies near the twinning-activation window, retention of fracture toughness is governed by whether crack-tip plasticity can activate deformation twins and stacking-fault–mediated hardening. When the effective SFE is lowered into this window, crack-tip nanotwinning and faulting sustain high strain hardening and crack-tip shielding, increasing toughness; when the SFE is higher and twinning is suppressed, slip is less accommodating, strain hardening diminishes, and toughness drops.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC high-/medium-entropy alloy with clean grain boundaries, no intentional precipitates, low interstitials, and a recrystallized grain size in the 10–50 µm range; SFE at room temperature close to the TWIP threshold (neither extremely high nor extremely low).
generation.intervention: Change test temperature (isothermal mechanical testing) to modulate the effective SFE without altering composition or grain size: compare room temperature to cryogenic temperature (e.g., 77 K) after identical solution anneal and quench.
generation.conditions: Plane-strain fracture tests (J–integral or K-based) at constant nominal strain rate (e.g., ~10^-3 s^-1) under air or inert gas, with the same prior solution treatment and cooling to minimize short-range order differences; microstructure verification before testing (XRD for single phase FCC, EBSD for grain size, TEM for absence of precipitates).
generation.structural_mediator: Crack-tip density and spatial extent of deformation twins and stacking faults (quantified in the crack-tip plastic zone), which are governed by the effective SFE at the test temperature.
generation.mechanism: Lower SFE at reduced temperature lowers the barrier for partial dislocation emission, promoting stacking faults and twin nucleation. Crack-tip nanotwinning increases strain hardening (back-stress and dynamic Hall–Petch effects), deflects/slows the crack, and enhances crack-tip shielding via distributed plasticity, delaying microvoid coalescence. At higher SFE, twins are suppressed; slip proceeds primarily by full dislocations with fewer obstacles to dynamic hardening, promoting earlier localization and lower fracture resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the room-temperature baseline, the cryogenic test will show: (i) a measurable increase in fracture resistance (J_Ic or K_Jc) beyond experimental scatter, (ii) a higher work-hardening rate in tension, (iii) greater crack-tip twin density and stacking-fault area fraction by TEM/EBSD-TKD, and (iv) more ductile, fine dimpled fracture with evidence of twin-related shear offsets near the crack path. If the SFE at room temperature is already too high for twinning, cooling should move it into a twinning-active regime and increase toughness; if it is already very low, cooling may not further increase toughness and may promote phase transformations instead (see boundary).
generation.baseline: Room-temperature plane-strain fracture toughness and tensile work-hardening behavior of the same alloy and microstructure (solution annealed, water quenched, same grain size).
generation.boundary: Applies to single-phase FCC HEAs/MEAs with SFE near the twinning window at room temperature, grain sizes above ~5 µm (to allow dislocation storage and twin propagation), and no brittle second phases. May not apply if: (a) the alloy is BCC or multiphase; (b) strong precipitation or pronounced short-range order dominates slip mode; (c) SFE is very high (twinning inactive even at cryo) or very low (ε/α' martensite or cleavage prone); (d) very high temperatures where dynamic recovery suppresses work hardening; (e) ultrafine/nanocrystalline grains wherein twinning is geometrically suppressed and toughness is governed by different constraints.
generation.uncertainty: The exact SFE–temperature dependence is composition-specific; some alloys may exhibit competing effects (e.g., short-range order evolution with temperature, or transformation-induced plasticity) that complicate the twinning contribution. The magnitude of toughness change cannot be predicted here without alloy-specific data. In alloys with strong planarity or precipitation hardening, cooling could increase strength but not toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of a single-phase FCC HEA/MEA with SFE near the twinning threshold at room temperature; solution anneal and water quench all coupons together to fix grain size and minimize compositional/ordering variations. Perform identical microstructural verification. Test half the coupons in plane-strain fracture at room temperature and half at 77 K. From companion tensile tests at both temperatures, extract work-hardening rates. Interrupt fracture tests just before instability to extract crack-tip foils for TEM/TKD to quantify twin and stacking-fault density in the plastic zone.
measurements: J_Ic or K_Jc with statistical replication at both temperatures
True stress–strain curves and instantaneous work-hardening rate (dσ/dε) vs ε
TEM/TKD quantification of crack-tip twin density and stacking-fault area fraction within a defined distance ahead of the crack tip
Fractography (dimple morphology, evidence of twin-related shear features)
EBSD kernel average misorientation maps to assess plastic zone extent
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after accounting for experimental scatter (e.g., 95% confidence intervals), the cryogenic condition does not show both (a) a higher fracture toughness than the room-temperature baseline and (b) a higher crack-tip twin/fault density, then the hypothesis is falsified. Observing equal or lower toughness at cryo with no increase in twinning/faulting would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
